title: Individual Hitters in College Softball
text:
Welcome to our college softball analytics website! Before analyzing team records and divisional differences, we begin with the fundamental building blocks of softball offense: the individual hitters.
Below are 2,175 individual NCAA Division I hitters from the 2022 season (minimum 100 plate appearances). We examine the relationship between on-base ability (OBP) and power (Slugging Percentage, SLG), shaded by total home runs hit.












Power and on-base skills rise together: Hitters who get on base at elite rates (.400+ OBP) also tend to slug significantly higher (.600+ SLG).
The impact of the long ball: Players in the highest home run tier (bright yellow points, 15+ HRs) dominate the upper-right quadrant of offensive production.
From individual hitters to team success: While individual hitters drive run production, does stacking home run power actually guarantee team victories across different divisions of college softball?

Explore our full findings across the site:

Check out the Story tab for a division-by-division analysis (D1, D2, D3, and JUCO) comparing home run rates to game outcomes.
Use the Exploration tab to interactively filter teams and examine the data yourself.

title: About This Project
text:
Project Background
This project investigates the relationship between home run hitting power and team winning success across collegiate softball divisions:

NCAA Division I
NCAA Division II
NCAA Division III
Junior College (JUCO / NJCAA)

It builds upon earlier milestones: - Milestone 3 (Team offensive metrics) - Milestone 4 (Individual Division I hitters) - Milestone 5 (Collegiate softball divisions analysis)

title: About This Project
text:
Data Sources

Individual Hitters: NCAA Division I hitting statistics compiled via the SCORE sports data repository and NCAA official softball stats (2,175 players with 100+ PA).
Collegiate Divisions: Team season statistics gathered from NCAA official statistics via softballR and NJCAA official softball statistics (1,286 collegiate programs).

This site was created using Quarto and R in VS Code.

title: The Story: Home Run Power vs. Game Outcomes
text:
After analyzing individual hitters on the homepage, our central research question turns to team performance: Does a higher team home run percentage lead to winning more games, especially when facing teams with lower home run production?
To answer this, we analyze 1,286 college softball teams across four divisions: - NCAA Division I (295 teams) - NCAA Division II (262 teams) - NCAA Division III (391 teams) - Junior College / NJCAA (338 teams)









Across all four levels, there is a clear, positive upward slope: teams that hit home runs at higher rates consistently win a higher percentage of their games.

text:
After analyzing individual hitters on the homepage, our central research question turns to team performance: Does a higher team home run percentage lead to winning more games, especially when facing teams with lower home run production?
To answer this, we analyze 1,286 college softball teams across four divisions: - NCAA Division I (295 teams) - NCAA Division II (262 teams) - NCAA Division III (391 teams) - Junior College / NJCAA (338 teams)









Across all four levels, there is a clear, positive upward slope: teams that hit home runs at higher rates consistently win a higher percentage of their games.

title: The Story: Home Run Power vs. Game Outcomes
text:
Division-by-Division Analysis

NCAA Division I










Statistical correlation: \(r = 0.52\), indicating a strong positive relationship.
Median benchmark: The median Division I team hit home runs in 1.96% of their at-bats.
Impact on game outcomes: Division I teams in the upper half of home run rate win 55.5% of their games, compared to just 42.7% for teams in the lower half — a 12.8 percentage point advantage.
Head-to-head dynamic: When a high-home-run D1 team plays a low-home-run opponent, the power advantage creates immediate multi-run innings against high-velocity pitching, shifting game odds heavily toward the power-hitting squad.




NCAA Division II










Statistical correlation: \(r = 0.42\).
Median benchmark: The median Division II team maintains a home run rate of 1.67%.
Impact on game outcomes: Teams above the median win 55.1% of their games, compared to 42.2% for below-median teams (12.9 percentage point advantage).
Head-to-head dynamic: In Division II, teams that maintain a 3.0%+ home run rate almost never finish below a .500 win rate. When facing lower-power teams, their ability to score without relying on stringing 3–4 consecutive singles together provides a reliable winning edge.




NCAA Division III










Statistical correlation: \(r = 0.48\) with the steepest regression slope (\(\beta = 11.9\)).
Median benchmark: The median home run rate in Division III is just 1.00%, the lowest of any collegiate division.
Impact on game outcomes: Teams above the median win 56.2% of their contests, while teams below the median win only 40.6% (15.6 percentage point advantage).
Head-to-head dynamic: Because power is so scarce in Division III, home runs act as a “super-weapon.” A single multi-run home run often decides an entire contest against an opponent that lacks home run capability.




Junior College (JUCO / NJCAA)










Statistical correlation: \(r = 0.57\), the strongest correlation among all divisions.
Median benchmark: The median JUCO team posts a 2.39% home run rate, the highest collegiate median.
Impact on game outcomes: Teams above the median win 55.1% of games, whereas teams below the median win just 32.6% — a massive 22.5 percentage point chasm.
Head-to-head dynamic: In the offensive-heavy JUCO environment, low-home-run teams struggle immensely to keep up on the scoreboard. When a higher-power team meets a lower-power team, the higher-power team wins nearly two-thirds of the time.

title: The Story: Home Run Power vs. Game Outcomes
section: Conclusion: Higher Home Run Percentage Decisively Impacts Game Outcomes
text:
Conclusion: Higher Home Run Percentage Decisively Impacts Game Outcomes
Across all 1,286 teams in college softball:

Consistent Advantage: In every division, teams in the top half of home run percentage win between 12.8 and 22.5 percentage points more games than teams in the bottom half.
Game Outcome Differential: When a high-home-run team plays a low-home-run team, the high-power team holds a substantial probability advantage. Power hitting generates unearned run potential, forces opposing pitchers into stressful counts, and turns deficits into leads with a single swing.
